ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The experiments were approved by the Bar-Ilan University Interdisciplinary Studies Unit ethics committee (approval numbers ISU202007003 granted on 14.08.2020 and ISU202208002 granted on 29.08.2022) and all research was performed in accordance with the ethics committee and the Declaration of Helsinki guidelines.

Participants were recruited via Prolific online platform (https://www.prolific.co/) with the following recruitment criteria: age (18-35 years old), fluency in English, credible participation experience on Prolific (at least 200 runs and acceptance rate of 98% and above), and participation with a desktop computer/laptop (not handheld devices).
table.formatted: Participants were recruited via Prolific online platform (<ref type="url" target="https://www.prolific.co/">https://www.prolific.co/</ref>) with the following recruitment criteria: age (18-35 years old), fluency in English, credible participation experience on Prolific (at least 200 runs and acceptance rate of 98% and above), and participation with a desktop computer/laptop (not handheld devices).

table.text: Each participant participated only once to ensure she/he were naïve to the study's memory aspects (for additional performance-based exclusion criteria see Analyses below).

While recruitment criteria and participant demographics were available via Prolific, the participants' identity was completely anonymized and we were blind to any identifying details (each participant was known by her/his Prolific-encrypted alphanumeric string).
Demographic data from Prolific was missing for one participant from the intentional memorization encoding experiment and for three participants from the naturalistic encoding experiment.
Prior to their participation participants were provided with an overall overview of the experiment as is common on Prolific.
All participants were paid at the end of their participation according to the criteria set by Prolific (regardless of their level of performance) and this was performed via the Prolific interface.
Participants were first presented with a demographics questionnaire (age range, gender, handedness, vision, and highest level of education).

The experiment started with the exposure phase where participants were asked to observe each image that appeared on the screen and follow any instructions that may appear (without any information about the memory aspect of the experiment that were to follow later).

During the exposure phase, 4 unexpected attention checks appeared (after every 32 images) where participants were asked to press the spacebar as fast as they could in order to continue the experiment (a black screen with the instructions "Press SPACE as fast as you can" appeared).

Participants were presented with surprise old-new recognition memory test instructions (to press leftward arrow if they recall seeing the image earlier or rightward arrow if not) and asked to press the shift key to proceed.
The experiment ended with an end of experiment screen and participants were then redirected back to Prolific with a completion code.

The procedures of this experiment were precisely as those of the naturalistic encoding experiment except for the instructions before the exposure phase where participants were asked to memorize the images they were about to see (see Fig. 1A).

table.text: Second, after each image presentation (2s, as in the other experiments), participants were presented with two image-content related sequential questions.
The participants were required to answer with no time restrictions.
(C) Test phase: after the exposure phase participants were given an old/new recognition memory test for sequentially presented 320 (160 old) intermediately-sized (8.5°) images.
Participants were required to report for each image if they recall seeing it earlier ("old") or not ("new").
In all three experiments, data of each participant were recorded in a CSV file and this included correctness and response times for each presented image.
Indeed, perceptual performance was at ceiling for the smallest images, indicating that participants were able to understand and correctly report the content of the images they saw.

The fact that perceptual measures were at ceiling indicates that participants were easily able to perceive and extract high-level visual information from the smallest images and therefore this cannot explain why they did not remember them as well as the larger images.
Participants were instructed to either view the images (naturalistic encoding experiment) or to memorize the images (intentional memorization encoding experiment).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.text: As was evident in the 2-way ANOVA analyses (see above), when examining only the effect of encoding task on overall memory, accuracy for already seen images was significantly affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 8.424, p = 0.000327, ŋG2 = 0.092; 1-way ANOVA) with higher overall accuracy in the perceptual encoding experiment relative to the naturalistic encoding experiment (p = 0.000442) but no difference between the accuracy in the intentional memorization encoding experiment and that of the naturalistic encoding experiment (p = 1).

Examining signal detection theory measures, memory sensitivity (dprime) was not significantly affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 1.893, p = 0.154, ŋG2 = 0.022) although there was a gradual increase in the mean memory sensitivity from lowest in naturalistic encoding to highest in perceptual encoding.

Decision criterion was, however, affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 3.461, p = 0.034, ŋG2 = 0.04) with lower overall criterion in the perceptual encoding experiment relative to the intentional memorization encoding experiment (p = 0.0479) but no difference between the decision criterion in the intentional memorization encoding experiment and that in the naturalistic encoding experiment (p = 1).

AUC was not significantly affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 2.988, p = 0.053, ŋG2 = 0.035) although mean AUC increased with encoding task in the same manner as memory sensitivity (dprime), and as can be seen in Figure 3E, AUC was significantly correlated with dprime in each of the experiments (naturalistic encoding experiment: r = 0.92, t(56) = 16.9, p = 1.05*10 -23 ; intentional memorization encoding experiment: r = 0.93, t(65) = 21.0, p = 1.28*10 -30 ; perceptual encoding experiment: r = 0.98, t(43) = 33.90, p = 1.17*10 -32 ).

As was evident in the 2-way ANOVA analyses (see above), when examining only the effect of encoding task on overall memory, accuracy for already seen images was significantly affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 8.424, p = 0.000327, ŋG2 = 0.092; 1-way ANOVA) with higher overall accuracy in the perceptual encoding experiment relative to the naturalistic encoding experiment (p = 0.000442) but no difference between the accuracy in the intentional memorization encoding experiment and that of the naturalistic encoding experiment (p = 1).

Examining signal detection theory measures, memory sensitivity (dprime) was not significantly affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 1.893, p = 0.154, ŋG2 = 0.022) although there was a gradual increase in the mean memory sensitivity from lowest in naturalistic encoding to highest in perceptual encoding.

Decision criterion was, however, affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 3.461, p = 0.034, ŋG2 = 0.04) with lower overall criterion in the perceptual encoding experiment relative to the intentional memorization encoding experiment (p = 0.0479) but no difference between the decision criterion in the intentional memorization encoding experiment and that in the naturalistic encoding experiment (p = 1).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------

"p's > .05"), Text = c("Repeated measures ANOVAs were performed using the R anova_test and get_anova_table functions where get_anova_table automatically applies the Greenhouse-Geisser sphericity correction only to factors violating the sphericity assumption (i.e., Mauchly's test significant p-value ≤ 0.05).", 
"No interaction between encoding task and image size on memory measures was found (all F's < 2, all p's ≥ 0.85, all ŋG2 ≤ 0.005).",

)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. table.text: We found an effect of image size on perception (F(3,132) = 12.8, p = 2.15*10 -7, ŋG2 = 0.060, 3° better than 6°: p = 0.00075, 6° similar to 12°: p = 1 and 12° lower than 15.5°: p = 0.011).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: There was also an effect of category-related task on perception (F(1,44) = 71.04, p = 9.86*10 -11, ŋG2 = 0.193) reflecting slightly higher performance on the person-related question (in red in Figure 2A) than on the place-related question (in blue in Figure 2A, p = 1.74*10 -15 ).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: An interaction between image size and category-related task on perception was found (F(3,132) = 21.87, p = 1.46*10 -11, ŋG2 = 0.121) and it likely reflected a small drop in performance in the person-related question in the 12° sized images, while for the place-related question there was a small drop of performance in the 6° sized images.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: We also found a significant effect of encoding task on accuracy of already-seen images and on decision criterion (but not on dprime) and these reflected significant increased accuracy and reduced criterion for perceptual encoding relative to both naturalistic or intentional memorization encoding experiments (accuracy: F(2, 167) = 8.42, p = 3.27*10 -4, ŋG2 = 0.072; criterion: F(2, 167) = 3.53, p = .031, ŋG2 = 0.038; dprime: F(2, 167) = 2.10, p = 0.125, ŋG2 = 0.022; see Table 2 for details).

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 7 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: We have recently found that during shallow ("naturalistic"/incidental) encoding larger images are better remembered.

However, it is unclear whether this reflects a genuine influence of image size on mnemonic processes or an epiphenomenal consequence of its influence on perception, and whether this effect robustly generalizes to deeper encoding.

Here, we tested these in three experiments (n = 189) differing in encoding depth: naturalistic (freely viewing the images without being informed a memory test will follow), intentional memorization (freely viewing while memorizing the images since a memory test was to follow), or perceptual encoding (reporting for each image whether there was a person in it and whether it was taken indoors or outdoors, without being informed a memory test will follow).
During encoding in the perceptual experiment, participants viewed 160 images of different sizes (3°-15.5°) followed by an old-new recognition memory test of 320 images (half "old").

While perceptual measures were at ceiling, memory improved with image size, presenting a dissociation between perception and memory and indicating that the effect of image size on memory is not a mere reflection of limited perception for smaller images.

Additionally, the effect of image size on memory generalized to all encoding tasks such that memory improved for larger images (as evident by accuracy and d'), regardless of average memory performance increasing with encoding depth.

These findings suggest that image size operates as a genuine sensory-based modulator of memory encoding, beyond perceptual sensitivity, pointing to a broader role of low-level visual properties in shaping memory representations.

While visual memory is not typically considered to be influenced by image size, we have recently found that during very shallow encoding (Craik & Lockhart, 1972) bigger images are better remembered for images sized 3-12 and this was evident both in the memory accuracy for already-seen images as well as in memory sensitivity (dprime) measures (Azrad et al., 2026; Kreichman et al., 2025; Masarwa et al., 2022).

text.text: However, the lower memory for smaller images we found may reflect degraded perception for smaller images.

In addition, there is a possibility that during very shallow encoding (e.g., during naturalistic (Azrad et al., 2026; Brook et al., 2024; Kreichman et al., 2025 Kreichman et al., , 2026;; Masarwa et al., 2022)) or incidental encoding (Bird, 1976; Castelhano & Henderson, 2005; Postman et al., 1955), physical image properties significantly influence visual memory, but that this influence diminishes during deeper encoding conditions when more attentional resources are devoted to process image content.

text.text: Here, we tested these in a set of experiments.

To test whether image size effect on memory reflects perception we obtained multiple per-image category-related perceptual measures in one of the experiments ("perceptual encoding") after which memory was also measured.
We assumed that if image size effect on memory reflects perception, then perceptual measures would also be influenced by image size.

To test whether the effect of image size on memory is specific to shallow encoding or generalizes to deeper encoding, we modulated the depth of encoding across three different experiments with encoding task varying from naturalistic (aka incidental (Bird, 1976; Castelhano & Henderson, 2005; Postman et al., 1955)), via intentional memorization, to perceptual encoding.

We found an effect of image size on perception (F(3,132) = 12.8, p = 2.15*10 -7 , ŋG2 = 0.060, 3° better than 6°: p = 0.00075, 6° similar to 12°: p = 1 and 12° lower than 15.5°: p = 0.011).

There was also an effect of category-related task on perception (F(1,44) = 71.04, p = 9.86*10 -11 , ŋG2 = 0.193) reflecting slightly higher performance on the person-related question (in red in Figure 2A) than on the place-related question (in blue in Figure 2A, p = 1.74*10 -15 ).

text.text: An interaction between image size and category-related task on perception was found (F(3,132) = 21.87, p = 1.46*10 -11 , ŋG2 = 0.121) and it likely reflected a small drop in performance in the person-related question in the 12° sized images, while for the place-related question there was a small drop of performance in the 6° sized images.

Overall, despite these statistically significant effects on perception, perceptual performance was very high, indicating that people were able to encode image information that allowed them to successfully judge image content even for the smallest images.

Examining signal detection theory measures, memory sensitivity (dprime) was not significantly affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 1.893, p = 0.154, ŋG2 = 0.022) although there was a gradual increase in the mean memory sensitivity from lowest in naturalistic encoding to highest in perceptual encoding.

Decision criterion was, however, affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 3.461, p = 0.034, ŋG2 = 0.04) with lower overall criterion in the perceptual encoding experiment relative to the intentional memorization encoding experiment (p = 0.0479) but no difference between the decision criterion in the intentional memorization encoding experiment and that in the naturalistic encoding experiment (p = 1).

In this study we found that image size effect on memory generalizes from shallower (naturalistic, aka incidental) to deeper (e.g. active perceptual) encoding tasks, and this cannot be explained by perceptual measures that were at ceiling already for the smallest images.

We have recently found that during naturalistic (shallower) encoding image size affects memory (Kreichman et al., 2025; Masarwa et al., 2022), but it is unclear whether this effect generalizes to more engaging and demanding (deeper) encoding conditions (i.e., different encoding tasks).

text.text: In these recent studies we have suggested (Kreichman et al., 2025; Masarwa et al., 2022) that the effect of image size on memory likely stems from the fact that visual system early processing stages, including retinotopic cortex, dedicate more resources to processing larger images (Tootell et al., 1997) and these eventually translate to higher quality signals transferred to higher visual and beyond visual memory areas (Felleman & Van Essen, 1991).

text.text: Since task has been shown to influence many levels of processing including early visual processing stages (Gazzaley & Nobre, 2012; Moran & Desimone, 1985; Reynolds & Chelazzi, 2004; Zhang & Luck, 2009), it is likely to modulate the effect of image size on memory.
text.formatted: Since task has been shown to influence many levels of processing including early visual processing stages <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gazzaley & Nobre, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Moran & Desimone, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Reynolds & Chelazzi, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Zhang & Luck, 2009)</ref>, it is likely to modulate the effect of image size on memory.

text.text: In addition, Craik and Lockhart (Craik & Lockhart, 1972) have suggested that memory is influenced by the depth of encoding and therefore it is possible that the physical aspect of image size only contributes to memory during shallow encoding, but that at deeper encoding other factors (e.g. top-down processes) play a much more important role (Harel et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In addition, Craik and Lockhart <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Craik & Lockhart, 1972)</ref> have suggested that memory is influenced by the depth of encoding and therefore it is possible that the physical aspect of image size only contributes to memory during shallow encoding, but that at deeper encoding other factors (e.g. top-down processes) play a much more important role <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Harel et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, it was unclear whether the effect of image size on memory generalizes to other and specifically deeper encoding tasks.

Here we found that when people are asked to memorize the images (intentional memorization while passively viewing the images) as well as when they are engaged in a highly demanding dual perceptual task, image size effect on memory is preserved.
Importantly, this is not a consequence of reduced perceptual measures for the smaller images.
Indeed, perceptual performance was at ceiling for the smallest images, indicating that participants were able to understand and correctly report the content of the images they saw.

While it is unclear whether the effect of image size on memory will generalize to additional, even more demanding encoding tasks, our results indicate that image size has a substantial effect on memory and this is not limited to very shallow encoding.
It has been suggested that larger images are better remembered since they are better perceived.
For example, it may be much easier to understand what is in a bigger image than deciphering the information of a very small image (Wolfe & Kuzmova, 2010).
text.formatted: For example, it may be much easier to understand what is in a bigger image than deciphering the information of a very small image <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Wolfe & Kuzmova, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: However, in our previous studies, since we relied on naturalistic encoding, we were not able to obtain any perceptual measures and therefore were not able to assess perception.
Here, we intentionally collected high-level per-image perceptual measures (with no involvement of or reliance on any working memory aspects from the previously seen images).
We assumed that if image size effect on memory is a consequence of poorer perception, then perceptual measures would also be modulated by image size.
However, here we found that perceptual measures were at ceiling already for the smallest image size, and yet memory performance was still affected by image size.

The fact that perceptual measures were at ceiling indicates that participants were easily able to perceive and extract high-level visual information from the smallest images and therefore this cannot explain why they did not remember them as well as the larger images.
Since perceptual qualia and experience are very rich and may not be captured by every specific task, it is hard to fully quantify how these are affected by image size.
Therefore, it is possible that other perceptual aspects that were not assessed here were influenced by image size.

Nevertheless, the dissociation we found between perceptual performance (not being influenced by image size) and memory (being influenced by image size) indicates that the effect of image size on memory cannot be fully explained by high-level perceptual measures.
There are several limitations that we must acknowledge.
As we mentioned above, we cannot rule out the possibility that additional encoding tasks not tested here will modulate and perhaps eliminate image size effect on memory.
We cannot also rule out the possibility that other perceptual measures not assessed here may explain to a certain extent the image size effect on memory.
In addition, our study included 160 images, and it remains to be tested whether these results will generalize to additional images.
Our findings were also obtained with young adults aged 18-35 years, and it is unclear whether these effects would replicate in younger or in older aged groups.
These limitations may be addressed in future research.

Taken together, our findings indicate that the contribution of image size to memory extends beyond shallow, naturalistic encoding to conditions involving deliberate, attentionally demanding processing, suggesting that this contribution is not limited to a single depth of encoding.

Beyond its theoretical relevance to accounts of encoding depth, this work may have important implications for policy makers, for educational purposes, for digital interfaces, and for increasing accessibility of information to elderly adults.
Future work should establish the boundary conditions under which physical image properties shape memory.
